turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry now, this computer's after freezing on me again. You're in for the knee, am I right?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): The knee, aye, but it's really the form. Warehouse want a line that I can still lift. The knee itself is only a small bit sore.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hang on, wrong chart. Say the form bit again?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): They want me signed off fit for the floor. I don't know, doctor, if ye even do those.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): We do. Which knee?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The right one. On the inside.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has that been at you?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. My wife filled the bit at the desk and put down three months, but she fusses.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And what would you say yourself?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Not three months. Two weeks, maybe three, the inside of that right knee. And I'm not limping, whatever she told your one outside.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): When do you feel it?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Going down the stairs, mostly. On the flat I'm grand. The car park was a nightmare, I nearly turned for home.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling, or does it lock, or give way?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. It doesn't lock. Giving way... no, it hasn't.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Painkillers?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, the odd time. Two tablets. I don't know, doctor, whether they do a thing.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything you take every day?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Atorvastatin, for the cholesterol. Twenty milligrams at night. I think. The box is at home, so I don't know.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twenty, you said?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I think it's twenty. Could be wrong. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the dose as twenty for now. Nurse put a pressure up... one hundred and seventy-eight over one hundred and two.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah here. Sure that's the white coat. I go sky high the minute I sit in that chair.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): There's a second reading, the screen hopped. Let me read it properly. One hundred and sixty-four over ninety-six.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that still bad?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's up, yeah. Any chest pain, headache, or shortness of breath with it?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None of that. I'm grand in myself.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only your wife has written breathless on the stairs on the form.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the knee catching, not the breathing. I'm not breathless. I don't know why she wrote that.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anyone in the family with pressure or strokes? I'm only asking while this loads.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had a stroke, years back. Smoked the whole time. I'm only mentioning it, it's not why I'm here.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough. Look, with those numbers I'm going to start ramipril, two point five milligrams at night, and see you in a month.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to? I was put on a pressure tablet before and I coughed the house down. I can't mind the name of it. They stopped it.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): An ACE inhibitor, was it? Ramipril, perindopril, one of those?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Years ago. Desperate cough, so that was the end of it.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, then I'm changing that. No ramipril. No new tablet today at all.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, I'd rather that.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll lend you a monitor from the surgery. Morning and evening, seven days, sitting quietly, write every reading down.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to buy one? I don't know, doctor, the chemist ones are dear.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): No, ours. Collect it at the desk on the way out and bring it back with the sheet.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): And will you still sign the work form?
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I've had a look there. No swelling on the knee, and it bends fully. I'll sign you for light duties only, no heavy lifting this next fortnight.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Light duties. The supervisor won't be delighted. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's the true line. This may well be white coat hypertension, so I'm not calling it high blood pressure for definite until the home numbers are in.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): So if they're high, then tablets?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): If they're high when you come back, then we talk about a tablet. Not before. Come back in a fortnight with the book.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I get a pain in the chest or a bad headache before that?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in sooner, or the emergency department if it's bad. Stay on the atorvastatin as you are. The pressure tablet is parked.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Doctor initially proposed ramipril 2.5 mg at night for raised blood pressure, but after the patient reported a previous severe cough with a prior blood pressure tablet/possible ACE inhibitor, the doctor explicitly changed the plan: no ramipril and no new blood pressure tablet today; the pressure tablet is 'parked'.
Patient reported previous blood pressure tablet caused a severe cough ('coughed the house down'); doctor considered this may have been an ACE inhibitor such as ramipril or perindopril.
Family history detail: father's stroke was years ago and he smoked heavily ('smoked the whole time').
Doctor instructed the patient to collect the surgery's blood pressure monitor from the desk on the way out and return it with the recording sheet.

There was a discrepancy between the wife's report and the patient's account: wife had written that he was breathless on the stairs, but the patient clarified it was the knee catching and denied being breathless.
Doctor had said 'see you in a month' when first planning ramipril, but after changing plan revised follow-up to a fortnight with the home blood pressure record.
